## Trainer

Choose **major** or **minor blues**, a **level**, and press **Start**. You hear three choruses of the blues, A, B and C, each in its own
band style. Two use the same changes; the third makes one different choice somewhere in the twelve bars. Which is different?
**Space** plays all three again, **A** / **B** / **C** answer, **N** shows or hides notation, **Enter** goes on.

<div id="blues-ear"></div>

**Bars** sets how much of the chorus you hear:

- **Four: the phrase with the change** (the default): bars 1–4, 5–8 or 9–12, whichever holds the difference. At levels 1–2 that is
  usually bars 1–4 (the quick change) or 9–12 (bar 10, the turnaround); at level 4 it is bars 1–4 or 5–8 (the passing chords); at
  levels 5–7 it is nearly always bars 9–12 (the turnaround). When a change runs across phrases (Bird changes at level 8), you hear
  the phrase where it starts.
- **Any four bars**: four bars in a row starting anywhere (bars 3–6, 8–11...), always including a bar that changes. The start is not a
  phrase start, so finding your place is part of the task.
- **All 12**: the whole chorus.
- **Bars I choose**: type the first and last bar (1–12). Questions are then made only from changes inside those bars; if no change at
  the level falls inside them (bars 1–4 at level 5, say), you are told so.

**Busyness** (under **The band**) calms the band down when a style gets too busy to hear the chords through: **Less busy** drops the
drum fills, has the bass play a two-feel (swing styles) or roots on beats 1 and 3, and the chords played steadily on the beat;
**Calm** holds each bass note and chord for its whole length over light brushes.

## What can change

A version of the blues is a set of choices on top of the basic twelve bars (in F: F7 for I7, Bb7 for IV7, C7 for V7):

| Where | The choices |
|---|---|
| Bar 2 | stay on I7, or the **quick change** to IV7 |
| Bar 4 | I7, or **v7 I7**, a ii–V into IV |
| Bar 6 | IV7, or **#iv°7**, a passing diminished chord leading back to I |
| Bar 8 | I7, or **VI7**, the V of ii |
| Bars 9–10 | **V7 IV7** (the blues way down), **V7 V7**, the jazz **ii7 V7**, or the **backdoor**: ii7, then iv7 bVII7 |
| Bars 11–12 | no turnaround, **V7** in bar 12, **I VI7 \| ii V**, or **I bIII7 \| bVI7 bII7** (the Tadd Dameron turnaround) |
| Tritone substitutes | **bII7** for the last V7, **bVI7** for the turnaround's VI7: the bass moves by semitone instead of by fifth |
| Bird blues | bars 1–10 as in Charlie Parker's "Blues for Alice": Imaj7, then ii–V's stepping down to IV, then down again to ii |
| Minor blues | i7 and iv7; bars 9–10 **bVI7 V7** or **iiø7 V7**; turnaround **V7** or **i bVI7 \| iiø7 V7**; **bII7** for the last V7 |

*Unverified:* these are the common jazz-blues reharmonisations as they are usually taught, written here from memory, and the Bird
changes are from memory of "Blues for Alice" (Parker, 1951). Neither is yet checked against a source.

## The levels

| Level | Counts as the same | What the different one changes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · The basic blues | style | the quick change in bar 2, or IV / V in bar 10 |
| 2 · Turnarounds | style | bars 11–12, or bar 10 |
| 3 · The jazz ii–V | 9ths and 13ths | V7 IV7 or ii7 V7 in bars 9–10; the turnaround |
| 4 · Passing chords | 9ths and 13ths | a ii–V into IV, #iv°7, or VI7 added or left out |
| 5 · Tritone substitutes | also 7b9, 7#9 on dominants | bII7 for V7, bVI7 for VI7 |
| 6 · Turnaround and backdoor | all the colours | backdoor, Tadd Dameron turnaround, tritone sub |
| 7 · Bird blues | all the colours | the turnaround after Bird changes |
| 8 · Anything | all the colours | any choice in any bar |

Minor blues has three levels: bar 2 and the turnaround; bars 9–10; substitutes.

Levels 1–2 use blues and rock styles (jump blues, boogie-woogie, rock, swing, doo-wop, Motown), with plain 7th chords. From level 4
the styles are jazz: swing, jazz ballad, bossa nova, boogaloo, stride. **The band → Styles** overrides this.

## Listening tips

- Count the bars. Most changes are in bars 2, 4–6, 8, or 9–12; mark where the chorus turns around.
- A tritone substitute keeps the same sound but slides: the bass goes down by semitone into I instead of by a fifth.
- **A tune on top** plays the same melody over all three choruses, so only the chords underneath change.
- **Notation** (block voicings with a bass line, and the tune when it is on) can be shown at any time; chord symbols appear after you
  answer, or always if you set **Notation → Chord symbols** to Always.
